common_name: Tanyosho Pine (Umbrella-Form Dwarf Japanese Red Pine)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Tanyosho pine develops its best orange-red bark and tightest umbrella form with full sun exposure and lean, well-drained soil.

directions: Tanyosho pine is a naturally dwarf, multi-trunked form of Japanese red pine that develops a broad, flat-topped, umbrella-like crown instead of the tall, irregular pyramid of the species, typically dividing into several trunks low to the ground while still young. Its trunks and upper branches show the same striking orange-red, plated bark as straight Japanese red pine, and the effect becomes more vivid as multiple trunks mature side by side over the years. Give it full sun and lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil, since rich, moist ground encourages soft, floppy growth that spoils its tight, sculptural silhouette. Little pruning is needed to maintain the umbrella shape, though candling off part of the new spring growth can be used to keep the crown dense and compact in a formal Japanese-style garden.

common_name: Dragon's Eye Pine (Yellow-Banded Variegated Japanese Red Pine)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; full sun exposure is essential for Dragon's Eye pine to display its yellow needle banding, which fades toward plain green in shade.

directions: Dragon's Eye pine is a variegated Japanese red pine selection named for the striking effect created when its paired needles are banded with two bright yellow rings, so that looking down on a branch tip reveals rows of concentric yellow-and-green circles resembling watchful eyes. The variegation shows best on new growth in full sun and can fade toward plain green in shadier positions or on older interior needles, so an open, sunny site gives the strongest display. It otherwise grows much like the species, eventually developing the same handsome orange-red, flaking bark and irregular, layered crown with age, though typically somewhat slower and more modest in ultimate size. Grow in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and avoid rich, wet ground, which encourages soft growth and increases susceptibility to pine wilt nematode in warm, humid climates.

common_name: Golden Weeping Willow (Tristis Yellow-Twig Weeping Willow)

planting.note: Plant hardwood cuttings or container-grown trees in early spring in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun near a pond, stream, or low-lying wet area; cuttings root readily and establish quickly.

directions: Tristis is the classic golden weeping willow, a fast-growing selection of white willow prized for slender, bright yellow young twigs that glow against bare winter branches and cascade in long, graceful curtains nearly to the ground. Its narrow, silvery-green leaves and pendulous habit make it one of the most recognizable weeping trees planted near ponds, lakes, and streambanks, where reflections double the effect of the sweeping canopy. Like the species it grows quickly into a large, wide-spreading tree and thrives in constantly moist to wet soil, but its aggressive, water-seeking roots must be kept well away from septic systems, water lines, and foundations. Prune out crossing or storm-damaged branches in late winter while the tree is dormant, and expect the cheerful yellow stem color to be most vivid on vigorous young wood.

common_name: Blue Pacific Shore Juniper (Low Silvery-Blue Coastal Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in sandy, well-drained, even infertile soil in full sun; Blue Pacific hugs the ground more tightly than most other shore juniper selections and tolerates salt spray and poor sandy soils with ease.

directions: Blue Pacific is among the lowest and most densely mat-forming of the shore juniper cultivars, hugging the ground at well under a foot tall while spreading steadily outward into a tight carpet of fine, silvery-blue needles. It takes on deeper steel-blue to purplish tones through cold winter months before returning to its summer blue-green color each spring. Like the species, it thrives in lean, sandy, fast-draining soil and shrugs off salt spray, wind, and drought once established, making it a dependable choice for seaside banks, dune stabilization, and hot parking-strip plantings where little else will grow. Avoid heavy, poorly drained soils and late-day overhead watering, both of which invite the fungal blights that can trouble junipers in humid climates.

common_name: Horstmann's Silberlocke Korean Fir (Compact Silver-Curl Korean Fir)

planting.note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist soil in full sun to partial shade; like 'Silberlocke', it prefers cool, humid conditions and struggles through hot, dry summers.

directions: Named for German conifer grower Gunther Horstmann, this selection is a denser, more compact sport of the popular Korean fir cultivar 'Silberlocke', carrying the same upturned needles that flash bright silvery-white undersides but on a tighter, slower-growing plant that stays well short of standard Silberlocke's eventual tree-like size. It forms a broad, dense, conical to irregularly rounded shrub rather than a single-leader tree, making it easier to fit into a foundation planting or smaller conifer collection while still showing off the two-tone silver-and-green needle display up close. Like its parent cultivar, it can begin setting ornamental, upright, purple-violet cones that fade to blue and brown while the plant is still relatively young and small. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade, providing the cool, humid conditions Korean fir needs, since it performs poorly through hot, dry summers.
